Senses.Explanation: To have a discerning eye: to be able to recognize, distinguish, or judge what an encounter puts forward. Danxia Tianran asks whether the person who fed a traveler has such an eye, and Muzhou Daoming asks the same about a donor after an unnamed participant returns from a meal. Fayan Wenyi explicitly tells an unnamed participant that his earlier question shows a discerning eye, then asks why he did not cover the exchange before the public assembly. Jiashan Shanhui gives the negative boundary: someone who depends on buddha-and-patriarch sayings as a model has not yet acquired the eye. Fayun Faxiu promises the eye if listeners can identify the color of the wind. Yuanwu Keqin asks those with the eye to judge whether Xuedou or the Buddha has exposed the other. Tiantong Hongzhi says an eye-equipped Chan participant will recognize and assent to his sequence of circle figures; Sanshan Lai says such a discerning guide departs as soon as the matter is raised. Mingjue Cong uses the forehead-eye expansion when he says the teaching seat should make each person discerning and impartial underfoot. Chan bends ordinary possession of sight into a public capacity that named speakers confer, question, demand, and test; it is not a physical-eye diagnosis and not automatic approval of every claim.

Senses.Explanation: To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents.
